title: Hummingbirds: Tiny Fliers
summary: How hummingbirds hover on fast-beating wings, feed on nectar, save energy at night, carry pollen between flowers, build tiny nests, and make long trips.
poll: A tiny animal can do things that big animals cannot.

versions.title: The Tiny Bird That Hums
versions.text:
Look at this bird. It is so small! It is a hummingbird. The least one is as long as your thumb. It weighs less than a coin.

Its wings move so fast. They beat fifty times a second. The wings hum. That is how it got its name.

This bird can hover. It can stay in one spot in the air. It can fly back, too.

It drinks nectar. It is a sweet juice. It is in a flower. The bird sips it. It has a long tongue.

It needs a lot of energy. Its heart beats fast. It must eat all day. At night, it gets cold. Its heart slows. That helps it last the night.

Pollen sticks to its head. The bird takes it to the next flower. That helps the plant make seeds.

The mom makes a nest. It is the size of half a nut. She uses spider silk. She lays two eggs.

Some of these birds fly far. One kind goes a long way. It flies over the sea. It does not stop.

They live in North and South America. None live in Saudi Arabia. But we have sunbirds. They sip nectar, too.

versions.title: Hummingbirds: Tiny Fliers
versions.text:
Imagine a bird that can stop in midair like a tiny helicopter. That is a hummingbird. These birds are some of the smallest on Earth. The bee hummingbird, the smallest species of all, is about as long as your thumb and weighs less than a small coin.

A hummingbird's wings move so fast that they look like a blur. Many kinds beat their wings more than fifty times a second. The rapid wings make a soft humming sound, which gives the bird its name.

Hummingbirds can hover, which means they stay in one place in the air. They can also fly backward and even sideways. Few other birds can control their flight so well.

These birds feed mainly on nectar, a sweet liquid inside flowers. A hummingbird pushes its long beak into a flower and laps up the nectar with its tongue. It also catches small insects and spiders, which give it protein.

Flying like this burns a lot of energy. A hummingbird's heart can beat more than a thousand times a minute. During the day, the bird must eat every few minutes. At night, it enters a deep, sleep-like state called torpor. Its body cools, and its heart slows down, which saves energy until sunrise.

As a hummingbird feeds, pollen brushes onto its head. When it visits the next flower, some of that pollen rubs off. In this way, the bird helps pollinate plants so they can make seeds.

The mother builds a nest about the size of half a walnut. She weaves it with spider silk, which stretches as the chicks grow. Inside, she lays two eggs about the size of beans.

Some hummingbirds migrate long distances. The ruby-throated hummingbird flies across the Gulf of Mexico without stopping, a trip of about 800 kilometers.

Hummingbirds live only in North and South America. Saudi Arabia has none, but it does have sunbirds, which also drink nectar from flowers.

versions.title: Hummingbirds: Masters of Flight
versions.text:
Imagine a bird that can pause in midair like a miniature helicopter, then dart backward before you can blink. That is a hummingbird, one of the smallest birds on the planet. The bee hummingbird, the tiniest of the more than three hundred species, measures about five centimeters long, roughly the length of a thumb, and weighs less than a small coin.

A hummingbird's wings move so rapidly that they appear as a blur to human observers. Many species beat their wings more than fifty times every second, and this rapid vibration generates the soft humming sound that gives these birds their name.

Hummingbirds can hover, which means they maintain a fixed position in the air while feeding, because their unusual shoulder joints allow the wings to twist and produce lift on both the forward and backward strokes. They can also fly backward and even sideways, a level of control that very few other birds possess.

These birds depend primarily on nectar, a sugary liquid that flowers produce to attract visitors. A hummingbird inserts its long, slender beak into a blossom and rapidly laps up the nectar with its tongue. It also captures small insects and spiders, which supply essential protein.

This extraordinary style of flight requires an enormous amount of energy, and hummingbirds have one of the fastest metabolisms of any animal. Their hearts can beat more than a thousand times a minute, so during daylight the birds must eat every few minutes. At night, they enter a deep, sleep-like condition called torpor, in which body temperature drops and the heartbeat slows dramatically, conserving precious energy until sunrise.

As a hummingbird feeds, pollen brushes onto the feathers of its head and is carried to the next flower, which makes the bird an important pollinator for many plants.

The mother constructs a nest about the size of half a walnut, binding the materials with spider silk that stretches as her chicks grow. Inside, she lays two eggs about the size of beans.

Some species undertake astonishing migrations. The ruby-throated hummingbird crosses the Gulf of Mexico without stopping, a journey of approximately 800 kilometers that requires it to store extra fat beforehand.

Hummingbirds live only in North and South America. Saudi Arabia has none, but it is home to sunbirds, which also drink nectar, although they usually perch rather than hover.

versions.title: Hummingbirds: Masters of Flight
versions.text:
Imagine a bird that can pause in midair like a miniature helicopter, then dart backward before an observer can even blink. That is a hummingbird, one of the smallest birds on the planet. The bee hummingbird, the tiniest of more than three hundred recognized species, measures approximately five centimeters, roughly the length of a human thumb, and weighs less than a small coin.

A hummingbird's wings oscillate so rapidly that they appear as an indistinct blur to human observers. Many species beat their wings more than fifty times every second, and this rapid vibration generates the distinctive humming sound that gives these remarkable creatures their name.

Hummingbirds can hover, maintaining a fixed position in the air while feeding, because their unusually flexible shoulder joints allow the wings to rotate and generate lift on both the forward and the backward strokes. They can also fly backward and even sideways, demonstrating a degree of aerial maneuverability that very few other birds possess.

These birds depend primarily on nectar, a sugary liquid that flowers manufacture to attract visitors, and a hummingbird extracts it by inserting its elongated, slender beak into a blossom and lapping repeatedly with its specialized tongue. It also captures small insects and spiders, which supply the essential protein that nectar alone cannot provide.

This extraordinary style of flight demands an enormous quantity of energy, and hummingbirds possess one of the fastest metabolisms of any animal, with hearts that can beat more than a thousand times a minute, so during daylight the birds must consume food every few minutes. At night, they enter a profound, sleep-like condition called torpor, in which body temperature declines considerably and the heartbeat slows dramatically, conserving precious energy until sunrise.

As a hummingbird feeds, pollen adheres to the feathers of its head and is subsequently transferred to the next flower it visits, which makes the bird an important pollinator for numerous flowering plants.

The mother constructs a nest approximately the size of half a walnut, binding the materials together with spider silk that stretches gradually as her chicks develop. Inside, she deposits two eggs approximately the size of beans.

Some species undertake astonishing seasonal migrations; the ruby-throated hummingbird, for example, crosses the Gulf of Mexico without interruption, an exhausting journey of approximately 800 kilometers that requires it to accumulate additional fat beforehand.

Hummingbirds inhabit only North and South America, so Saudi Arabia has none, but the kingdom is home to sunbirds, which similarly drink nectar, although they typically perch rather than hover.

checklist: I explained why hummingbirds use so much energy.
I described two ways they get or save energy.
I used details from the article to support each point.
MID.modelAnswer: A hummingbird uses a huge amount of energy because its wings beat more than fifty times a second so it can hover in one spot while it feeds. One way it deals with this is by eating nectar every few minutes all day long to refuel its body. Another way is by entering torpor at night, a deep sleep-like state where its heart rate slows down and its body cools, which saves energy until morning.

keyWords.definition: all the chemical processes a body uses to turn food into energy
keyWords.example: Exercise can speed up your metabolism for a few hours.

keyWords.definition: a deep, sleep-like state in which an animal's body temperature and heart rate drop to save energy
keyWords.example: Some desert mice enter torpor on cold winter nights.

keyWords.definition: a regular journey that animals make from one region to another
keyWords.example: The migration of the birds brought thousands of them to the wetlands.

keyWords.definition: an animal that carries pollen between flowers, helping plants produce seeds
keyWords.example: The honeybee is the best-known pollinator on many farms.

keyWords.definition: a group of living things of the same kind that can breed together
keyWords.example: Scientists discovered a new species of frog in the rainforest.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Hummingbirds are in danger because their migrations are too long.
Hummingbirds' small size, fast metabolism, and unusual flight shape how they feed, rest, and travel.
Hummingbirds are found on every continent, including Asia.
Hummingbirds are mainly hunters of insects and spiders.
questions.why: The article connects the bird's tiny body and fast metabolism to hovering, frequent feeding, torpor, and migration.

wrong.A: The article does not say hummingbirds are in danger.
wrong.C: The article says they live only in North and South America.
wrong.D: Nectar is their main food; insects add protein.

questions.stem: According to the article, what allows a hummingbird to hover?
options: Hollow beaks that weigh almost nothing at all
Tiny feet that grip the air
A long tongue that balances its body
Flexible shoulders that let the wings twist
questions.why: The article explains that flexible shoulder joints let the wings rotate and make lift on both the forward and backward strokes.

wrong.A: The article does not mention hollow beaks.
wrong.B: Feet do not grip the air.
wrong.C: The tongue is used for lapping nectar, not balance.

questions.stem: As used in the article, metabolism most nearly means
options: the rate at which a body uses energy
the careful way a bird builds its nest
the speed of a bird's migration
the color of a bird's feathers
questions.why: The article links a fast metabolism to a racing heart and the need to eat every few minutes, which shows it is about using energy.

wrong.C: Migration speed is not what metabolism means.

questions.stem: Why does the ruby-throated hummingbird store extra fat before crossing the Gulf of Mexico?
options: To stay warm if it lands in the water
To look larger to enemies
It cannot stop to feed on the 800-kilometer flight.
Mexico has no flowers with nectar.
questions.why: The bird crosses without stopping, so it must carry stored energy as fat for the whole trip.

wrong.A: The article does not say it lands in the water.
wrong.B: The article does not mention looking larger.
wrong.D: The article says nothing about Mexico lacking flowers.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the description of torpor?
options: Hummingbirds sleep more than any other bird.
Torpor makes hummingbirds fly faster the next day.
Without torpor, a hummingbird might run out of energy before sunrise.
Torpor happens only during long migrations.
questions.why: The bird cannot feed at night, and torpor lowers its temperature and heartbeat to conserve energy until it can eat again.

wrong.A: The article does not compare sleep times among birds.
wrong.B: The article does not say torpor increases speed.
wrong.D: The article describes torpor happening at night, not only during migration.

questions.stem: Why does the author begin by comparing a hummingbird to a miniature helicopter?
options: To help readers picture its hovering flight
To explain how helicopters were invented
To suggest that hummingbirds are noisy machines
To show that hummingbirds fly very high
questions.why: Like a helicopter, a hummingbird can stay in one place in the air and change direction, so the comparison creates a clear picture.

wrong.B: The article is not about the history of helicopters.
wrong.C: The comparison is about movement, not noise or machines.
wrong.D: Helicopters hover; the comparison is not about height.

questions.stem: How do sunbirds differ from hummingbirds, according to the article?
options: Sunbirds do not drink nectar.
Sunbirds live only in the Americas.
Sunbirds are larger than most eagles and hawks.
Sunbirds usually perch instead of hovering.
questions.why: The article says sunbirds also drink nectar but typically perch rather than hover.

wrong.A: The article says sunbirds also drink nectar.
wrong.B: Sunbirds live in Saudi Arabia; hummingbirds live only in the Americas.
wrong.C: The article does not compare sunbirds with eagles.

questions.stem: Why does the article call the hummingbird an important pollinator?
options: It eats insects that harm flowers.
It carries pollen on its head from flower to flower.
It plants the seeds of flowers near its own nest.
It drinks the extra water from flowers.
questions.why: Pollen sticks to the feathers on its head and is transferred to the next flower it visits.

wrong.A: The article does not say the insects it eats harm flowers.
wrong.C: The bird does not plant seeds.
wrong.D: It drinks nectar, and that is not why it is a pollinator.

HIGH.prompt: The hummingbird's greatest strength, its flight, also creates its greatest challenge. Explain this idea using at least three details from the article.
checklist: I explained what makes hummingbird flight special.
I explained the challenge its flight creates.
I supported my explanation with at least three details from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: A hummingbird's flight is its greatest strength because its rapid wingbeats let it hover, fly backward, and even move sideways, skills almost no other bird has. However, this remarkable flight comes with a serious challenge, since such constant hovering demands an extremely fast metabolism that forces the bird to eat every few minutes during the day just to survive. To cope with this challenge, the hummingbird enters torpor at night to slow its racing heart and save energy, and some species even manage a nonstop migration of about 800 kilometers across the Gulf of Mexico despite their tiny size.
